analytic.title: Orchestration of heterogeneous, distributed, real-time control containers

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In today's global market, manufacturers must be highly adaptable, producing profitably smaller batches. Disintegrating hardware and software and embracing modern IT concepts like containerization and Service-oriented Architecture enable this flexibility. While offering rapid reconfiguration, these approaches add complexity. Orchestration tools aid in analyzing response times, workload mapping, and parameter selection for containerized real-time applications. However, current tools struggle with managing distributed, heterogeneous, real-time apps. This paper proposes an orchestration solution based on Compositional Performance Analysis and Genetic Algorithm to optimize task allocation across diverse computing resources. The approach enables the orchestration of heterogeneously scheduled, container-based, distributed real-time systems.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In the context of the contemporary marketplace, the capacity to rapidly and seamlessly adapt manufacturing systems to accommodate customizable, new products in ever smaller batches is paramount for the sustained profitability and competitiveness of any enterprise [1]. Software Defined Manufacturing (SDM) can offer a solution by enhancing the flexibility within manufacturing systems [2]. At the core of SDM lies the principle of decoupling software and hardware [2,3]. However, to realize SDM, a compatible software and hardware architecture is needed, which enables the dynamic reconfiguration of real-time systems' software [4].

service-oriented architecture (SOA)s decompose monolithic architectures into smaller components, making the system as a whole more flexible [5]. In contrast to a single system encompassing the entire functionality, smaller, loosely coupled components are composed to realize the application. Deploying the individual services as containers provides high flexibility, and portability [6]. As shown in [7] containers can in principe be used as deployment units for real-time services. Nevertheless, real-time requirements inherent to manufacturing applications challenge existing virtualization technologies, as they generally do not inherently support real-time [8]. Popular existing container technologies such as Docker 1 or Kubernetes 2 require non-trivial extensions to be able to achieve real-time behavior [9,10]. 1 available at https://www.docker.com/ 2 available at https://kubernetes.io/ Orchestration platforms provide tools for deploying and managing complex service architectures consisting of multiple containers or virtual machines (VMs) hosted on multiple compute nodes. A multitude of application types are employed in industrial manufacturing, including Computerized Numerical Control (CNC), Robot Operating System 2 (ROS2), IEC61499, and Programmable Logic Controller (PLC). While orchestration solutions exist for individual manufacturing application types, no comprehensive solution is available. This complicates the administration of such systems, potentially leading to situations where a specific application type must be used, even when an alternative may be better suited to the use case. A fundamental property of real-time software running industrial manufacturing hardware is the Worst Case Response Time (WCRT), i.e. the maximum time needed for a system to react to an input event. Upper-bounding the WCRT is a well-studied subject of research, but its application for real-time orchestration is limited to single computing nodes or homogeneous real-time systems.

The contribution of this paper consists of the extension of a manual orchestration tool developed in previous work [11] to support the automated orchestration of heterogeneous distributed real-time systems. Based on a description of the distributed system and resources, i.e., CPU schedulers, workloads are assigned to compute nodes and compute cores, using a genetic algorithm, which minimizes the WCRTs.

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section II-A covers technical fundamentals surrounding real-time computing and distributed systems. Section II-B presents a review of existing real-time orchestration solutions and response time analysis approaches. Section III introduces the concept developed in this paper, aiming to extend the analysis capabilities and enable real-time orchestration. The implementation is described in Section IV. Subsequently, Section V focuses on the evaluation. Section VI discusses the evaluation and limitations of the approach. Finally, Section VII concludes the paper with a summary and potential future research directions.

div.head: II. BACKGROUND
div.p: The subsequent subsections introduce the fundamental concepts of response time analysis, distributed systems and container orchestration, before outlining the state of the art. A. Fundamentals

div.head: 1) Response time analysis:
div.p: To analyze the response time of a real-time system, one important property is the Worst Case Execution Time (WCET) of the involved tasks. The WCET is an upper-bound for the time required to execute a task. As estimating the WCET is an active research topic of its own [12], in this paper, the WCET of a task is assumed to be known and no effort will be made to estimate it.

The Worst Case Transmission Time (WCTT) is analogous to the WCET. It is concerned with the duration of communication between tasks. The primary metric the orchestration of this paper is concerned about is the WCRT. It upper-bounds the time between activation and completion of a task. Unlike the WCET, WCRT considers numerous task activations and potential interference from other tasks, providing a more comprehensive assessment of real-time system behavior on a shared computing resource. The WCRT can be extended to reason about chains of tasks, also called flows. Instead of only reasoning about a single task, the time between activating the first task in the flow and completing the last in the flow is considered [13].

2) Virtualization and orchestration: There are several ways to realize virtualization as illustrated in Figure 1. As containers can be well explained by comparing them to VMs, we first introduce VM-based virtualization. A hypervisor is a piece of software responsible for creating and running the VMs. It interfaces with the underlying host computer to provide the virtual abstraction of system resources, such as CPU and Random Access Memory (RAM) to each VM. Containerization removes the need for a full VM with virtual hardware and dedicated operating system. A container contains all dependencies to run independently and is directly executed in the host's operating system, isolated from other tasks using control groups and namespaces. Containers are assigned only the required resources, and privileges [14].

Orchestration of distributed systems means the automatic configuration, management, and deployment of VMs, containers, or other SOA components [14]. Most orchestration tools enable developers to specify the desired state of the system via declarative models to automate the deployment. These models define what type of components should be created, and how many resources they are assigned [15]. One widely used orchestration solutions is Kubernetes, which is able to manage containerized distributed systems at a large scale [14].

div.head: B. State of the Art
div.p: The following section reviews the state of the art regarding real-time container orchestration. It observes that existing orchestration solutions do not generally support real-time systems. Furthermore, existing research analyzing the behavior of real-time systems is also considered.

1) Real-time containers and orchestration: An extended overview of of real-time containers can be found in [16,17]. Open challenges for real-time container adaptions identified by [16] are the need for container management tools and the ability to expose the requirements of applications running in the containers to enable an efficient allocation of resources, i.e. orchestration. Kubernetes is a widely used open-source container orchestration system. It does not innately support the administration of real-time containers but can be extended to do so. For instance, [9] presents a software architecture able to deploy independent real-time containers with Kubernetes. Similar approaches are [18], [8], and [19]. The latter two consider the allocation of shared memory and cache in addition to the CPU. An extension to the Linux Kernel is presented in [20], which extends the existing scheduling policies by hierarchical container-based scheduling to guarantee temporal isolation of containers sharing a CPU, which only requires the definition of real-time quotas on container levels, rather than on thread level. However, this scheduling model does not consider communication latencies and WCRTs of flows. Nevertheless, the extension is widely used in other research [8,9,18,21].

ROS2 is a software framework for building robot applications capable of real-time. The Kubernetes-based orchestration platform specifically tailored to ROS2 KubeROS is presented in [22]. Similar, FogROS2 [23] is a platform supporting the cloud deployment of ROS2. One of the main goals of FogROS2 is to improve performance and latency of ROS2 applications. However, it is unclear if real-time applications are feasible with FogROS2.

IEC 61499 applications can be orchestrated using the methods provided by [24]. A microservice and container-based architecture is used to automatically deploy services in an edge computing environment. The authors note that most but not all real-time constraints can be met, as response times under 1ms are challenging to achieve with the proposed system. Another orchestration solution for IEC 61499 applications is presented in [25]. A simple application is developed to validate the platform, but no analysis of the system's real-time properties is conducted.

Container technology for CNC systems is explored in [26]. System modules are split up and deployed into containers to enable parallel execution. The real-time performance in the virtual environment is tested and worse than in conventional deployment but still capable of controlling CNC machines. PLC runtimes are deployed into containers and orchestrated by Kubernetes in a microservice architecture in [27]. The dynamic orchestration enables fast and dynamic changes, such as bug fixes or software updates, in PLC systems. Moving PLC runtimes between nodes is also possible, as the changes can be carried out fast enough not to interrupt the normal system function. A test application shows that PLC containers meet real-time requirements. However, the communication latencies between PLCs are not considered.

div.head: 2) Response time analysis approaches:
div.p: We select Compositional Performance Analysis (CPA) [28] as an analysis tool for the WCRT of the containerized, heterogeneous real-time applications. CPA is an analysis approach to determine the end-to-end latency of heterogeneous distributed systems [28]. This is enabled by CPA through a compositional approach. Each method analyzes a homogeneous subpart of the system. Their partial results are then used to estimate the response time for the whole system. For the remainder of this paper we adopt the CPA system model of [29]. According to [29] a system is a network of resources that provide processing time and tasks that consume it. Containers are groups of tasks. All tasks that are executed on one resource share the same scheduling algorithm. Several communicating tasks can form a chain [13]. In a chain, a task is dependent on its predecessor's response to start execution. Thus, a chain of tasks can be seen as a directed acyclic graph. As described in Section II-A, in the context of this paper the WCRT describes the maximum of an input event to propagate through the system of acyclically connected tasks.

Figure 2 illustrates the iterative approach of CPA. The system model generates the initial event models based on the arrival curves of inputs and provides context for the local analysis methods. In each iteration, the local analysis methods produce derived output event models. These derived event models propagate through the system to be used as input models. This process continues until a result for the WCRT is obtained or resources are overload. Otherwise the system is deemed not schedulable.

3) Research Gap: In conclusion, several orchestration solutions for real-time applications are proposed in the literature but cannot be used to orchestrate containerized, heterogeneous, distributed real-time applications. They are exclusively focused on administrating a single application type. Furthermore, most approaches rely on the independent task model and do not consider the WCRT of chained services. Some approaches are also focused on deployment in the cloud, posing a significant challenge to guaranteeing real-time requirements.

div.head: III. DESIGN OF THE ORCHESTRATION
div.p: First, this section presents the concept and design of the approach to analyze the distributed heterogeneous real-time application based on CPA. Afterward, the design of a genetic algorithm (GA) is presented that optimizes the assignment of tasks to resources.

div.head: A. Response time analysis
div.p: A system in this paper is considered to be composed of a set of n heterogeneous resources R = r 1 , ..., r n . Each resource represents a CPU or CPU partition capable of executing tasks using a scheduling model. Supported scheduling methods include static priority preemptive scheduling (SPPS), static priority non-preemptive scheduling (SPNPS), time-division multiple access (TDMA) based scheduling, round-robin and hierarchical or server-based scheduling. The reasoning behind this is, that SPPS, TDMA and SPNPS are used for many PLC and CNC applications and hierarchical scheduling enable the isolation of resource on the container rather than the thread level [8]. Due to the usage of the CPA approach, the number supported scheduling methods can be extended easily. A resource is characterized by the parameters affecting the scheduling algorithm. This can be either the specification of a linear supply bound function [8], specified by quota and period, or a TDMA based supply bound function specified by bandwidth, period and slot size.

A system contains a set of m different tasks T = t 1 , ..., t m . The workload of a task is defined by its WCET. We use the periodic, jitter, minimum distance (PJD) event model to describe input events, as other commonly used event models can be transformed into this model as presented by [31]. Further parameters of a task are the scheduling parameters, e.g., the priority of a task in a SPPS system. Tasks are permanently bound to their resources and global scheduling algorithms is not supported, as global scheduling schemes tend to introduce higher scheduling overhead and context switch overhead [32].

The communication links between tasks are modeled using the WCTT. Each task, that is not first in its chain, has exactly one predecessor from which it receives its event model through the CPA propagation. This predecessor can either be another task or a junction node. A junction node combines two or more communication connections into one [28]. An OR-junction generates one output event for each input event, while an AND-junction generates one output event only after receiving an incoming event from all of its predecessors.

div.head: B. Design of the orchestration and analysis system
div.p: The goal of the analysis system is to integrate a CPA based approach with a real-time container orchestrator. Figure 3 provides a visualization of the conceptual architecture. The orchestration application calls the analysis module, i.e., the CPA module for real-time analysis. The CPA component's analysis result can fall into one of two categories. If the system is schedulable, it returns the WCRT of every task in addition to a WCRT value for every flow. A flows WCRT is the sum of the WCRT of every involved task and the WCTT of every involved communication link. A final load distribution on the resources at the time convergence is also included. If the system is not schedulable, an error instead of the WCRT is returned, as no event model can be derived from tasks on an unschedulable resource.

div.head: C. Task to resource mapping with a Genetic Algorithm
div.p: The ability to automatically analyze real-time properties of a modeled system enables automated system optimization. A approach is task allocation to minimize response time, a challenge described as NP-hard [33,34]. A GA based on ImGA [34] is utilized to tackle the mapping problem, albeit not necessarily providing optimal solutions. The following sections describe each of the steps the GA goes through to create solutions for mapping tasks to resources. The major difference to [34] are consideration of flows instead of independent tasks and the combination with CPA in addition to the below highlighted adjustments to the GA itself.

1) Genome: The genome, i.e., the solution encoding, is a dictionary with resource types as keys and arrays of lists as values, the indices if the arrays are the cores. The cores contain lists of tasks assigned to them. The operators of the GA are independently applied to resources of the same scheduling type. In contrast ImGA uses a flat array as only one scheduling type is supported.

2) Fitness function: The fitness function of ImGA, that assigns high scores to high numbers of schedulable tasks, is completely replaced. The GA aims to minimize the system's response time by creating a task-to-resource mapping. The fitness function assigns higher scores to solutions with lower response times. The default fitness function, denoted as f , sums the WCRT of all system tasks. Consequently, the approach is framed as a minimization problem.

The WCRTs of mapped tasks are derived as described above, evaluating the real-time behavior of the solution's described system. If a solution specifies a non-schedulable mapping, it receives a static maximum score exceeding any valid solution, e.g., the maximum integer value.

An alternate version of the fitness function is provided to the GA upon user request, which minimizes the WCRT of flows instead of independent tasks. This variant exclusively considers the WCRT of specified flows, excluding other tasks from score calculation. Nevertheless, the impact of these tasks on the system remains integral to optimization, as they could potentially interfere by sharing resources or influencing input event models of flow tasks. A limitation of the model is the assumption of static, sufficiently pessimistic WCTT between two tasks, which cannot be meaningfully optimized as it remains constant regardless of task mapping. However, we assume a Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN)-based network to be used. Thus, a Central Network Configuration can be used to calculate time slots for communication based on the allowed WCTT. The mapping is considered unusable if the Central Network Configuration cannot fulfill a WCTT.

div.head: 3) Solution representation and model transformation:
div.p: The GA takes a system definition as input, extracting necessary information for its operation, including details on computing resources and tasks within the application. The solution's genome represents task-to-resource assignments in a heterogeneous application. Resources are grouped by type, ensuring tasks are assigned to resources of the same type. The resource type corresponds to the scheduling type of the core, such as SPPS. Figure 4 shows the genome of a solution example. There, 10 tasks, represented by circles, are mapped to 8 different resources. In the example, resources 0 to 3 are of type SPPS and 4 to 7 of type SPNPS.

div.head: 4) Generation of the initial population:
div.p: The effectiveness of a GA heavily relies on the initial population [34,35]. The initial population generation in this paper follows a twostep process. Initially, tasks are randomly assigned to valid resources based on their type. However, when task workload nears resource capacity, many solutions may overload resources, rendering the system non-schedulable. It is preferable to restrict these invalid solutions early on as they do not contribute to achieving the goal. Therefore, a set number of random solutions are chosen for enhancement, aiming to shift them towards a schedulable mapping, inspired by the local search proposed in [36]. Our algorithm transfers some randomly selected task from overloaded resources to random resources with available capacity of the same resource type. The number of how many tasks are transferred before the algorithm moves on to the next potential initial solution is a configurable parameter. The load is determined by CPA. In this initial step the objective is not to generate solutions with particularly good scores but rather to obtain a higher number of valid initial solutions.

div.head: 5) Generating the next generation:
div.p: The new generation's genome is derived from the fittest solutions of the previous generation. New solutions are generated in one of two ways. The first method is elitism selection, i.e., transferring a set of solutions with the best scores directly to the new generation. Additional next-generation members are generated through the recombination of two existing solutions, followed by potential mutation. Recombination candidates are drawn from the mating pool, which includes reasonable solutions from the current generation, including elite ones. The crossover operator combines the genomes of two solutions to create a new one, followed by mutation in a specified percentage of solutions to maintain diversity. Further details are elaborated below.

Tournament selection identical to ImGA is employed to determine which solutions contribute to the new generation. It randomly selects individuals from the population for a tournament, from which the fittest individual is chosen to join the mating pool. Offspring for the next generation are then generated from this pool through crossover and mutation.

Various implementations of crossover operations exist in the literature, often tailored to specific problem types and solution encodings [37]. The core concept remains consistent ImGA. The algorithm selects two solutions randomly from the mating pool and recombines their genomes. In the subsequent steps, the better solution is referred to as S 1 and the inferior one as S 2 .

Step 1: The mutation begins by copying the resourceto-task-mappings of the resource with the least load from S 1 to the offspring. Then, the algorithm selects the mappings of remaining resources with the least load from S 2 . This process repeats until no more resources can be selected. If a mapping contains a task is already assigned to a previously selected resource, this task is removed from the mapping. Leftover tasks are handled in Step 2.

Step 2: The tasks leftover from the recombination in Step 1 are assigned according to a score based ratio between the parent solutions' scores. The main adjustments made to [34] is the extension to support multiple scheduling types. Furthermore, in contrast to ImGA the loads are not updated after every execution of Step 1, as CPA is expensive (see Section V).

The mutation process initially randomizes task assignments while maintaining resource task counts, then exchanges tasks between the busiest and least busy resources for each resource type [34]. Futhermore, in ImGA a circular permutation on arrays is performed, whereas here, new tasks are assigned semi-randomly.

Stagnation is mitigated by counting the number of generations the fittest solution has not changed. After reaching a threshold a paramtriziable number of solutions is replaced by new random solutions. In contrast ImGA uses the hamming distance between two solutions, because its solutions are encoded as arrays.

div.head: 6) Finding the best solution:
div.p: The algorithm terminates if it reaches the maximum number of generations or surpasses a threshold without finding a better solution. Several aspects of the GA presented in this chapter are highly configurable. [34].

div.head: IV. IMPLEMENTATION
div.p: This section presents the prototypical implementation of the concepts presented above. RT-Lang from previous work [11] is used to model the real-time applications. RT-Lang implemented as a Visual Studio Code extension, models and analyzes real-time applications modeled graphically or textually using a custom Domain specific language (DSL). Flows are automatically analyzed, including the e2e value representing the WCRT, as shown in Figure 5. For the analysis, the pyCPA python module 3 provides an open-source implementation of CPA [38].
Figure 6 visualizes the system architecture of the prototypical implementation. 3 available at https://github.com/ida-tubs/pycpa

Several features are added to RT-Lang [11] as part of the implementation. First, the RT-Lang approach is extended so that all information required by the system model presented in Section III-A is supported. The Validator component is also reworked. In addition to the previously supported analysis methods, the CPA approach is added. For this, the Validator passes on the system description to the CPA Module, implemented in this paper. The GA presented in chapter 4 is also implemented. For the provided model of a distributed real-time application, the GA generates a task-to-resource mapping. This solution is then transformed to Kubernetes deployment files through RT-Lang, i.e., deployments with container-to-node, task-to-core, and partition affinities and configmaps that pass the scheduling parameters into the applications.

div.head: V. EVALUATION
div.p: The prototypical implementation presented in the previous chapter is evaluated based on its performance in orchestrating randomly generated systems.

There are three size variants of random systems: 1) Small system: consisting of 4 resources and between 8 and 20 tasks, divided among 8 chains. 2) Medium system: consisting of 8 resources and between 16 and 40 tasks, divided among 16 chains. 3) Large system: consisting of 16 resources and between 32 and 80 tasks, divided among 16 chains. The first tasks incoming event model is a randomly determined PJD model with the following parameters: P ∈ [1000, 2000], J = P 2 and D ∈ [1, P 2 ]. Each task has a random value priority value in [1,100] and WCET ∈ [5,100]. This results in a load on each resource between 0.05 and 0.75. Each system contains resources scheduled according to two different scheduling algorithms. Each resource is randomly assigned one of the two selected algorithms. The first two resources are assigned different scheduling algorithms to ensure the presence of multiple schedulers. Each performance evaluation is performed on a computer with an AMD Ryzen 5 5600H CPU. All other applications or OS services are stopped or limited as much as possible during the evaluation to limit interference.

div.head: A. Response time analysis evaluation
div.p: Random systems of each size variant are generated and then analyzed to evaluate the response time analysis of the implemented CPA approach 100. All systems are ensured to be schedulable. The execution time is measured between the start and end of the analysis. The time to read and transform the model is not measured. However, during the evaluation process, the time taken up by model transformation and other preliminary setups is negligible.

1) Performance and system size: Figure 7 shows the performance evaluation results for each of the three system size variants. The median execution time for small, medium, and large systems is 0.13s, 0.25s, and 0.71s, respectively. The large systems show the highest spread of results. Outliers are not shown in this figure. Instead, Figure 8 visualizes outliers. A value is considered an outlier if it is larger than the upper whisker or smaller than the lower whisker of the box plot. The data contains no lower outliers, only upper ones. The outlier values measured are significantly larger than the median execution times, particularly for small and medium systems. The longest recorded execution time for a small system is 4.58 seconds, more than 30 times longer than the median value. The most significant outlier in medium systems is 20 times larger than the median, and in large systems, only 4.8 times. Notably, the outlier values of the different systems exhibit a greater degree of similarity in size compared to the average values.

2) Investigation of outliers: The performance evaluation reveals several very significant outliers. Re-running the analysis does not significantly change the outlier values. A closer inspection reveals a common trait among the most egregious outliers. All the resources contain at least one task assigned to them with an extremely high WCRT compared to their WCET. This behavior can be observed for all evaluated scheduling algorithms. Notably, overloaded systems do not exhibit this significant computation time increase. When generating 100 small random systems purposely overloaded, an analysis time of less than 1ms is observed.

div.head: B. Genetic Algorithm evaluation
div.p: Random systems of each size variant are generated to evaluate the performance of the implemented GA 10. Table I shows the parameters used to configure the GA. For all systems, a schedulable result is found. The execution time is measured from the start of the initialization of the first generation to the return of the best solution found. Figure 9 shows the performance evaluation results for the GA. Even the small system's median runtime is 433s, increasing to 779s for medium systems and 2539s for large systems. In addition to performance, the number of new best solutions in a generation is tracked. Every time the current best solution is replaced, it is tracked. Figure 10 visualizes when new best solutions are found. For all system sizes, the most new solutions are found in the 0th generation, i.e., the initially generated population. This is not surprising since the first generations are least fit. As the number of generations increases, the number of new solutions decreases. Only some improvements have been found in the last generations for small and medium systems. In contrast, for large systems, the discovery of the best new solutions remains relatively constant until the maximum generation is reached.

div.head: VI. DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS
div.p: This chapter examines results obtained by the previous implementation and evaluation. The findings are interpreted, and the limitations of the approach are highlighted. The implemented CPA based approach can analyze systems in a timely manner. The evaluation shows that the execution times for large systems remain close to 1s. Using this analysis method in an orchestration tool would provide quick insight into the system's response time. The need to wait about 1s seems reasonable for users of such a tool. Should the system size be much larger or analysis take longer, a possible solution would be to split the system into several distinct components. Then, the analysis could be run individually for each of them. The discovered outliers systems indicate that the analysis performance is more than strictly dependent on system size. Instead, the ease of scheduling also plays an important role. Systems where a very high relative WCRT take up significantly more computing resources. Some limitations of this paper's response time analysis approach need to be highlighted. First, modeling real-time systems simplifies the WCTT to a static value. While this is reasonable if sufficiently pessimistic WCTTs are chosen, this can be improved in future work Real-time calculus or a similar approach could be used for this [39].

As the evaluation shows, the GA can find task assignments and improve upon them to minimize the WCRT of the system. When considering the runtime of the CPA implementation and the GA, the former is the computationally more expensive part of the algorithm. One reason possibly lowering the overall GA performance is the sporadic long execution time of the CPA for some similar systems. When a solution generated by the GA specifies such a system, it would severely impact the time to evaluate a generation. By removing such solutions, the 0 500 1,000 1,500 2,000 2,500 3,000 small medium large time in seconds performance flaw could be eliminated.

Tuning the parameters of GA is a complex undertaking but essential. Suitable parameter configurations can significantly impact a GA's performance and result quality [40]. As part of this paper, only a minimal tuning process is carried out. The configuration is primarily adapted from the GA presented in [34]. While a similar problem is solved there, the specific implementation and problem definition varies. Another limitation of the system model arises from the GA. WCET of tasks are statically defined by being sufficiently pessimistic. This means that the GA operates under the assumption that the WCET of a task is the same on every resource. However, different resources might operate at different clock speeds, resulting in different WCET.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: A critical part of orchestrating heterogeneous, distributed real-time applications is the assignment of tasks to their computing resource. Manual assignment is tedious for larger applications. For this reason, this paper introduced a combination of CPA and a GA to optimize task distributions. A modeled real-time application serves as the input, and the output is the best assignment of tasks to resources the GA could calculate given its specified parameters. The result is not guaranteed to be optimal but available in a far shorter time frame. The performance of the GA could be improved in several ways. First, the main computational load is highly parallelizable. Every member of the next generation could be generated and evaluated in parallel. Thus, a high speedup could be achieved, depending on the number of available CPUs. By caching solutions that reappear frequently throughout the run of the GA, the time to analyze them could be saved. In summary, this paper presents an GA to optimize the assignment of tasks to computing resources by minimizing the systems WCRT. Both contributions were prototypically implemented and evaluated.
